## Course objectives

Students will be able to:

- apply statistical knowledge to analyze data and answer biological questions
- communicate and report data visually, orally, and in writing
- apply their knowledge to areas of personal interest such as conservation, sustainability, and health
- identify racist and colonial legacies in biostatistics and ways to positively intervene to stop the perpetuation of those legacies 


# What is statistics?

## What is statistics?


> Statistics is the study of methods to describe, measure, and test hypotheses about nature from samples. Statistics gives us tools to *describe the uncertainty* of measurements and the scientific insights we seek to gain from those measurements.

## What is statistics?

Comes down to one question:

> Sure?

## Goals of statistics

1.  Estimation
2.  Hypothesis testing

## Biology is messy

Three sources of variation:

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
    \item{Measurement error}
    \item{Random variation}
    \item{Complexity}
  \end{itemize}
```
Adapted from www.statstree.org

## Biology is messy

```{=tex}
\begin{exampleblock}{Measurement Error}
    No measurement device is perfect \\
    More precise tools are better \\
    e.g. digital stopwatch versus second-hand on an analog clock
  \end{exampleblock}
```

## 1. Know why and how biologists use statistics

### You should be able to:

-   Define statistics as the measurement of uncertainty and pursuit of insights in light of uncertainty
-   Describe sources of uncertainty
-   Describe uncertainty in terms of \alert{probability} and \alert{distributions}
-   Describe the goals of statistics as \alert{parameter estimation} and \alert{hypothesis testing}
-   Formulate parameters to estimate and statistical hypotheses to test
-   Distinguish between a \alert{population} and a \alert{sample}
-   Distinguish between a \alert{parameter} and an \alert{estimate}




## What is statistics?

> Statistics is the study of methods to describe, measure, and test hypotheses about nature from samples. Statistics gives us tools to *quantify the uncertainty* of measurements and the scientific insights we seek to gain from those measurements.

## What is statistics?

Comes down to the question:

> Sure?

## Goals of statistics

1.  Estimation
2.  Hypothesis testing

## \alert{Estimation}

> \alert{Estimation} is the process of inferring an unknown quantity of a \alert{population} using \alert{sample} data

-   \alert{Population}: all individual units in a collective (e.g. trees in a forest, cells in a body, genes in a genome, etc.)

-   \alert{Sample}: a subset of the population

## Parameter vs. Estimate

> A \alert{parameter} is a quantity describing a \alert{population}, whereas an \alert{estimate} or a \alert{statistic} is a related quantity calculated from a sample

-   \alert{Parameter}: the "Truth" about a \alert{population}

-   \alert{Estimate} (aka \alert{Statistic}): what we calculate from a \alert{sample} that represents our best guess of the parameter value


## Parameters


```{r echo=FALSE}
d <- data.frame(c("average", "proportion", "variation", "relationship"),
                c("the average mass of a certain bird species",
                  "the proportion of fertile seeds in a fruit",
                  "the variance in leaf area within a tree",
                  "the relationship between latitude and species diversity"))
names(d) <- c("Parameter type", "Biological example")
knitr::kable(d, escape = FALSE, format = "latex")
```

## \alert{Pause \& Think}: Distinguishing \alert{Samples} and \alert{Populations}

Example: *Uhu body size*

1. What is the \alert{population}?
    - There's some ambiguity to it
    - Could be all the "uhu" in the classroom (we just extirpated the population...not ethical)
    - Could be all the uhu in near shore O\`ahu waters
    - Could be all the uhu that could hypothetically ever exist given current conditions
2. What is a \alert{sample}?
    - Depends to an extent on our choice of how we define population
    - Could be the data from *one section* 
    - Could be the data from *all sections combined* (but only if we don't define the population as all the "uhu" in the classroom)

## \alert{Pause \& Think}: Distinguishing \alert{Estimates} and \alert{Parameters}

Example: *Uhu body size*

1. What would be a useful \alert{parameter} to describe some aspect of the population?
2. What is the \alert{estimate} of that parameter?

## \alert{Pause \& Think}: Distinguishing \alert{Estimates} and \alert{Parameters}

Example: *Uhu body size*

1. What would be a useful \alert{parameter} to describe some aspect of the population?
    - mean (aka average, aka expected value) of body length
2. What is the \alert{estimate} of that parameter?
    - estimate is our best guess of the true, unknowable parameter value 
    - we make this "guess" with the data from our sample


## Sources of variation

```{=tex}
\begin{exampleblock}{Measurement error}
    No measurement device is perfect \\
    More precise tools are better \\
    e.g. digital stopwatch versus second-hand on an analog clock
  \end{exampleblock}
```
```{=tex}
\begin{exampleblock}{Random variation and sampling error}
    We can't control everything \\
    There's always some random noise we can't eliminate \\
    e.g. temperature fluctuates affect biological processes
  \end{exampleblock}
```
```{=tex}
\begin{exampleblock}{Complexity}
    We can't measure everything \\
    Many environmental, genetic, and other factors affect biology \\
    e.g. a person's upbringing, environment, genetics could affect drug efficacy
  \end{exampleblock}
```


## Hypothesis testing

A \alert{scientific hypothesis} is a proposition about how the world works

A \alert{statistical hypothesis} is a specific claim regarding a population parameter. 

A \alert{statistical hypothesis} is related to but generally more specific than a scientific hypothesis




## Comparing scientific and statistical hypotheses

Example: **Uhu body sizes**

\alert{Scientific hypotheses} are propositions about how the world works

\vspace{0.25cm}

> Uhu have gotten smaller in waters around Hawai`i due to over-harvest and pervasive ecosystem degredation.

\alert{Statistical hypotheses} are related, but specific about population parameters

\vspace{0.25cm}

> The mean length of the contemporary uhu population is smaller than the historical baseline mean of 550 mm ($(\mu_\text{now} - \mu_\text{past}) < 0$)

# 2. Explain variables in your data

### You should be able to:

-   Define \alert{variable}
-   Distinguish \alert{categorical}, \alert{numerical}, and \alert{ordinal} variables
-   Distinguish \alert{explanatory} and \alert{response} variables

## What is a \alert{variable}?

> \alert{Variables} are characteristics that could differ among individuals or other sampling units

## We distinguished \alert{categorical}, \alert{numerical}, and \alert{ordinal} variables

> \alert{Categorical} data are qualitative characteristics of individuals that do not have magnitude on a numerical scale

> \alert{Numerical} data are quantitative measurements that have magnitude on a numerical scale

> \alert{Ordinal} data are qualitative measurements, but ordered

## \alert{Explanatory} vs. \alert{Response} variables

Variables can be either \alert{explanatory} or \alert{response} variables

\alert{Explanatory} variables are hypothesized to cause, directly or indirectly, a change in a \alert{response} variable

## \alert{Explanatory} vs. \alert{Response} variables

Typical notation:


```{r echo=FALSE}

tibble(
  Symbol = c("$Y$", "$X$", "$X_1, X_2$"),
  Variable = c("Response", "Explanatory (e.g. $Y = \\beta_X X$)",
               "Multiple explanatory (e.g. $Y = \\beta_1 X_1 + \\beta_2 X_2$)")
) |>
  knitr::kable(escape = FALSE, format = "latex")
```


Just because a statistical model says $X$ "causes" $Y$, it doesn't necessarily mean it's true

# 3. Randomly sample a population

### You should be able to:

-   Know that a good sample is *precise* and *unbiased*
-   Distinguish the \alert{precision} and \alert{bias} of a sample
-   Know that a \alert{random sample} involves *equal chance* and *independence*
-   Identify sources of bias in a nonrandom sample


## Why sample?

We don't have time, budget, ability to measure every unit in a population

## \alert{Pause \& Think}: Random and indipendent samples

Example: **Uhu body sizes**

1. If we treat all the "uhu" scattered around the classroom as the \alert{population} and the data collected by each of the 5 sections as 5 \alert{samples}, are the samples \alert{random}?
2. Are the samples \alert{independent}?
3. What types of processes or mistakes could lead to non-random and/or non-independent samples?

## Why do we care?

Whether or not samples are \alert{random} and \alert{indipendent} impacts the reliability of our answer to the foundational question: **Sure?**

That happens due to:

- Inaccurate assessment of uncertainty: non-random and non-independent samples artificially decrease uncertainty
- Change in precision
- Change in bias 



## Properties of a good sample

-   We cannot eliminate biological variation or sampling error
-   The best we can do is produce *precise* and *unbiased* estimates

![](img/ws1-2-2.jpg)

## Precision versus bias

These sets of estimates are equally precise, but the first is *biased*

| **Biased** | Estimate | Parameter | Error      |
|------------|----------|-----------|------------|
|            | 2        | 1         | 2 - 1 = +1 |
|            | 3        | 2         | +1         |
|            | 4        | 3         | +1         |
|            | 5        | 4         | +1         |

| **Unbiased** | Estimate | Parameter | Error      |
|--------------|----------|-----------|------------|
|              | 0        | 1         | 0 - 1 = -1 |
|              | 3        | 2         | +1         |
|              | 2        | 3         | -1         |
|              | 5        | 4         | +1         |

## Obtaining good samples

-   Decreasing variance increases precision

    -   Reduced measurement error

-   Large samples increase precision by decreasing sampling error

-   But very precise measurement and large samples can still be biased!

    -   In fact, large sample size reinforces bias

-   Random sampling leads to unbiased estimates

## \alert{Random} samples

A sample is random if two criteria are met:

1.  Every unit in the population has an \alert{equal chance} of being sampled

2.  The probability that one unit is sampled is \alert{independent} of another unit being sampled

## \alert{Random} samples

```{=tex}
\begin{columns}
\column{0.5\textwidth}
  \metroset{block=fill}

  \begin{alertblock}{Pause \& Think}
  Suppose you are running a clinical study to document the effect of noni juice on arthritis management. Your treatments are {\tt YES noni} and {\tt NO noni}. You allow clinical subjects to choose their treatment and to switch between treatments such that some of the data points in the {\tt YES noni} and {\tt NO noni} treatments come from the same people 
  \end{alertblock}
  
\column{0.5\textwidth}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item These samples are not random and independent: self-selection and repeated \alert{units of replication}
  \item Could cause \alert{bias} from self-selection and repeated measurements; and increased \alert{variance} from repeated measurements
  \item Solution: randomly and independently assign treatments!
  \end{enumerate} 

\end{columns}
```

# 4. Organize data in a spreadsheet

## 4. Organize data in a spreadsheet

### You should be able to:

- Organize data into a spreadsheet that is machine- and human-readable following principles of Broman & Woo (2018)

## "The Great Recession"

\includegraphics[width = 4in]{img/unemployment-rate.png}

##  Policy responses to "The Great Recession"

1. Governments should go into debt to temporarily increase economic demand
    - e.g. American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA)
2. Governments should NOT go into debt because it would cause economic growth (GDP) to decline
    - key evidence for effect of debt on growth came from [Reinhart \& Rogoff (2010)](https://10.1257/aer.100.2.573)
  
##  Reinhart \& Rogoff (2010) argued that GDP stops growing when government debt hits 90\% of GDP

\includegraphics[width = 2.5in]{img/reinhart-rogoff-2010-fig2.png}

## An error in Excel caused the apparent decline at 90\% of GDP

\includegraphics[width = 2.75in]{img/reinhart_rogoff_coding_error_0.png}

Source: https://qz.com/75119/how-to-avoid-making-an-excel-mistake-like-rogoff-and-reinhart/

## No major decline in GDP Growth when debt exceeds 90\%

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# From Herndon et al. (2013)
# http://peri.umass.edu/fileadmin/pdf/working_papers/working_papers_301-350/WP322.pdf

df = tibble(
  `Public Debt/GDP Category` = c("0-30%", "30-60%", "60-90%", "Above 90%"),
  `With error` = c(4.1, 2.9, 3.4, -0.1), # Reinhart & Rogoff 2010
  `Without error` = c(4.2, 3.1, 3.2, 2.2) # Herndon et al. 2013
) |>
  pivot_longer(-`Public Debt/GDP Category`, values_to = "Real GDP Growth (%)",
               names_to = "Data analyzed:") |>
  mutate(highlight = `Public Debt/GDP Category` == "Above 90%")

ggplot(df, aes(`Public Debt/GDP Category`, `Real GDP Growth (%)`, fill = `Data analyzed:`, alpha = highlight)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
  scale_alpha_discrete(range = c(0.5, 1)) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

```

## Organize your data and show your work

* Without data organization and validation, anyone can make serious statistical errors
* Organize your data: adopting the correct principles will help you avoid serious errors
* Show your work: a script shows *exactly* which steps you took and allows anyone else to reproduce your work

## Activity: Identify at least two deviations from the principles of Broman \& Woo (2018)

- Consistent codes for categorical variables
- Uses NA for missing data where applicable
- Consistent variable names
- Consistent subject identifiers
- Dates written in YYYY-MM-DD format
- No leading or trailing white space
- No empty cells
- One item per cell
- Data are rectangular
- No calculations in raw data file
- No font color or highlighting as data
